title: The global energy balance as represented in CMIP6 climate models
field: Global energy balance in climate models
problem: State-of-the-art CMIP6 climate models exhibit substantial inter-model spread in representing key components of the global energy and water balance, highlighting persistent discrepancies despite improvements in multi-model mean values compared to earlier generations.
method: This study investigates the representation of the global energy balance in 40 CMIP6 climate models by comparing their simulated energy budget components against recent observational and satellite-derived reference estimates to assess their performance and historic development.
task: The task is to investigate the representation of the global energy balance in 40 state-of-the-art global climate models participating in the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 6 (CMIP6) and compare it with reference estimates.

innovation: This paper assesses the global energy balance in 40 CMIP6 models, demonstrating that the multi-model mean largely remediates a long-standing bias of overestimated surface shortwave and underestimated downward longwave radiation, bringing the simulated surface radiation budget into closer agreement with recent reference estimates.

kg_extraction_triplets.paragraph: It was only with the advent of space-based measurements that the shortwave (solar) and long-wave (thermal) energy exchanges between Earth and space could finally be quantified adequately, particularly through the Earth Radiation Budget Experiment (ERBE, Barkstrom et al. 1990) in the late 1980s and the more recent Clouds and Earth's Radiant Energy System (CERES, Wielicki et al. 1996) mission since the beginning of the 2000s.

It was only with the advent of space-based measurements that the shortwave (solar) and long-wave (thermal) energy exchanges between Earth and space could finally be quantified adequately, particularly through the Earth Radiation Budget Experiment (ERBE, Barkstrom et al. 1990) in the late 1980s and the more recent Clouds and Earth's Radiant Energy System (CERES, Wielicki et al. 1996) mission since the beginning of the 2000s.

However, the inter-model spread in the representation of many of the components remains substantial, often on the order of 10–20 Wm¯² globally, except for aspects of the shortwave clear-sky budgets, which are now more consistently simulated by the CMIP6 models. The substantial inter-model spread in the simulated global mean latent heat fluxes in the CMIP6 models, exceeding 20% (18 Wm¯²), further implies also large discrepancies in their representation of the global water balance.

The model-output variables under consideration for this study are the shortwave and longwave radiative fluxes at the surface and the TOA under both all-sky and clear-sky conditions, as well as the non-radiative fluxes of surface sensible and latent heat. They stem from the “historical all forcings" experiments of CMIP6, which aim at simulating the climate evolution since preindustrial times as realistic as possibly, considering all major natural and anthropogenic forcings, namely changes in solar output, atmospheric greenhouse gases, aerosol loadings (tropospheric and stratospheric volcanic), and land use (Eyring et al. 2016).

In this mission, filtered radiances in the shortwave (between 0.3 and 5 µm), total (0.3 and 200 µm), and window (8 and 12 µm) regions are measured on board of the NASA satellites Terra and Aqua, with longwave radiances determined as differences between total and shortwave channel radiances.

In this mission, filtered radiances in the shortwave (between 0.3 and 5 µm), total (0.3 and 200 µm), and window (8 and 12 µm) regions are measured on board of the NASA satellites Terra and Aqua, with longwave radiances determined as differences between total and shortwave channel radiances.

The uncertainty of the outgoing longwave flux at the TOA as measured by CERES due to the uncertainty in calibration is ~3.7 W m¯² (2 σ), whereas the uncertainty in the short-wave reflected flux is ~2% (2 σ), or equivalently 2 Wm-2 (Loeb et al. 2009).

The uncertainty of the outgoing longwave flux at the TOA as measured by CERES due to the uncertainty in calibration is ~3.7 W m¯² (2 σ), whereas the uncertainty in the short-wave reflected flux is ~2% (2 σ), or equivalently 2 Wm-2 (Loeb et al. 2009).

This is consistent with current best estimates from space-based observations of 1361 Wm-2 (Kopp and Lean 2011) provided by the NASA Solar Radiation and Climate Experiment (SORCE). There remain, however, a few models which still use a solar constant that deviates substantially from the 1361 Wm-2.

At the time of the revision of this manuscript (March 2000), data from simulations performed by 40 GCMs appropriate for the present analysis have become available from CMIP6. They stem from the “historical all forcings" experiments of CMIP6. (Note: BCC-CSM2-MR is one of the 40 GCMs listed in figures such as Fig. 1, which display the results from these experiments).

kg_extraction_triplets.paragraph: The gradual upward adjustment in the simulated present-day shortwave absorption in the cloud-free atmosphere over the history of model development has been favored by the inclusion of absorbing aerosol in the radiation codes of the models [the early models did only consider sulfur-based scattering aerosols, or did not consider aerosols at all, e.g., Cusack et al. (1998)].
